text: Wald distribution (also known inverse Gaussian distribution) describes first-passage time Wiener process (Brownian motion drift) single absorbing boundary. context decision-making, models time takes evidence accumulate decision threshold. shifted Wald distribution adds non-decision time component account processes like stimulus encoding motor response execution: \[ RT = T_{decision} + T_{ndt} \] \(T_{decision}\) follows Wald distribution \(T_{ndt}\) non-decision time. probability density function shifted Wald : \[ f(t | v, , \tau) = \frac{}{\sqrt{2\pi (t-\tau)^3}} \exp\left(-\frac{(- v(t-\tau))^2}{2(t-\tau)}\right) \] \(t > \tau\), : \(v\) drift rate (rate evidence accumulation) \(\) boundary (decision threshold) \(\tau\) non-decision time

title: The Censored Shifted Wald Model (cswald)
text: ’ll simulate data multiple participants individual differences drift rates, demonstrating fit hierarchical models bmm: Let’s visualize RT distributions participant:
code: # set seed for reproducibility set.seed(42)  # simulate data for 3 participants in two conditions n_subjects <- 5 n_per_condition <- 200  # fewer trials per condition to keep file size manageable  # Population-level parameters pop_drift_A <- 3.0      # mean drift for condition A pop_drift_B <- 1.8      # mean drift for condition B drift_sd <- 0.5         # between-subject SD in drift bound <- 1.5            # shared boundary ndt <- 0.3              # shared non-decision time  # Generate subject-specific drift rates subject_drifts_A <- rnorm(n_subjects, pop_drift_A, drift_sd) subject_drifts_B <- rnorm(n_subjects, pop_drift_B, drift_sd)  # Simulate data for each subject and condition dat_list <- list() for (i in 1:n_subjects) {   # Condition A   dat_A <- rcswald(n = n_per_condition,                     drift = subject_drifts_A[i],                     bound = bound,                     ndt = ndt)   dat_A$id <- paste0("S", i)   dat_A$condition <- "A"      # Condition B   dat_B <- rcswald(n = n_per_condition,                     drift = subject_drifts_B[i],                     bound = bound,                     ndt = ndt)   dat_B$id <- paste0("S", i)   dat_B$condition <- "B"      dat_list[[2*i-1]] <- dat_A   dat_list[[2*i]] <- dat_B }  # Combine all data dat <- do.call(rbind, dat_list) dat$id <- factor(dat$id) dat$condition <- factor(dat$condition)  # Check error rates by subject and condition error_rates <- aggregate(response ~ id + condition, data = dat,                          FUN = function(x) mean(x == 0)) print(error_rates) #>    id condition response #> 1  S1         A    0.025 #> 2  S2         A    0.020 #> 3  S3         A    0.015 #> 4  S4         A    0.010 #> 5  S5         A    0.020 #> 6  S1         B    0.075 #> 7  S2         B    0.010 #> 8  S3         B    0.130 #> 9  S4         B    0.020 #> 10 S5         B    0.065 ggplot(dat, aes(x = rt, fill = factor(response))) +   geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, position = "identity", alpha = 0.7) +   facet_grid(id ~ condition, labeller = labeller(     condition = c(A = "Condition A", B = "Condition B")   )) +   scale_fill_manual(values = c("0" = "red", "1" = "blue"),                     labels = c("0" = "Error", "1" = "Correct"),                     name = "Response") +   labs(x = "Response Time (s)", y = "Count",        title = "RT distributions by participant and condition") +   theme_classic()

title: The Censored Shifted Wald Model (cswald)
text: want estimate: Population-level effects: drift rate varies condition Individual differences: Random effects drift rate participant Shared parameters: Boundary non-decision time constant across participants formula includes fixed effects condition random effects (varying intercepts) participants: (0 + condition | id) term drift formula specifies random slopes condition participant. allows model estimate: population-level drift rate condition Individual deviations population means condition variability (SD) correlation individual differences across conditions hierarchical structure provides several advantages: Partial pooling: Individual estimates pulled toward group mean, providing stable estimates participants less data Uncertainty quantification: model quantifies within- -subject variability Shrinkage: Extreme individual estimates regularized toward group mean
code: formula <- bmf(   drift ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),  # fixed condition effects + random subject effects   bound ~ 1,                          # shared boundary   ndt ~ 1                             # shared non-decision time )

title: The Diffusion Decision Model (ddm)
text: Diffusion Decision Model (DDM) one widely used cognitive models analyzing response time (RT) accuracy data two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) tasks. Originally developed Ratcliff (1978), DDM become cornerstone cognitive psychology neuroscience research decision-making processes. DDM ideal : RT data two-choice decision task correct error responses want decompose decision-making separate cognitive processes need account speed-accuracy tradeoffs want model trial--trial variability decision processes ’re interested linking cognitive parameters neural behavioral measures bmm package provides single DDM specification default fixed starting point. include formula zr bmf() call, starting point becomes freely estimated parameter. Trial--Trial variability parameters DDM currently supported, due feasibility Bayesian hierarchical estimation.

title: The Diffusion Decision Model (ddm)
text: DDM models decision-making noisy accumulation evidence time toward one two decision boundaries. evidence accumulation process described Wiener diffusion process: \[ dX(t) = v \cdot dt + s \cdot dW(t) \] : \(X(t)\) accumulated evidence time \(t\) \(v\) drift rate (average rate evidence accumulation) \(s\) within-trial noise (standard deviation diffusion process, typically fixed 0.1 1) \(dW(t)\) Wiener process (Brownian motion) process starts position \(z \cdot \) (\(z\) starting point parameter \(\) boundary separation) continues reaches one two absorbing boundaries 0 (lower/incorrect) \(\) (upper/correct).

text: Starting point bias (\(z_r\)): Relative starting point evidence accumulation (0 = lower boundary, 1 = upper boundary). Default: fixed 0 (implies \(z_r = 0.5\) response scale) Interpretation: priori response bias

title: The Diffusion Decision Model (ddm)
text: full DDM, described Ratcliff McKoon (2008) implemented Henrich et al. (2024) STAN, includes three additional parameters capture trial--trial variability core parameters: Drift rate variability (\(s_v\) sdrift): -trial variability drift rate, accounting fluctuations evidence quality across trials (typical range: 0 2). Non-decision time variability (\(s_{t_0}\) sndt): -trial variability non-decision time, accounting variable encoding/motor times (typical range: 0 0.2). Starting point variability (\(s_z\) szr): -trial variability starting point, accounting variable response bias across trials (typical range: 0 0.5). 7-parameter version implemented bmm: variability parameters theoretically important can improve model fit, Henrich et al. (2024) demonstrated 7-parameter likelihood prohibitively long computation times, especially hierarchical Bayesian estimation. Key limitations include: Single-subject feasibility : Even 100-300 trials, model fitting can 20 minutes using within-chain parallelization. 1500+ trials typical robust DDM estimation, runtimes likely extend hours even days. Hierarchical models infeasible: common use case cognitive research (multiple subjects, conditions, trials) becomes computationally intractable without high-performance computing resources. typical hierarchical study (20+ subjects, 2-3 conditions, 200+ trials per condition) likely require weeks computation time. Limited practical benefit: research questions, fixed- free-starting-point models provide adequate fits interpretable parameters, making substantial computational cost 7-parameter version difficult justify. researchers specifically interested trial--trial variability parameters, recommend considering simulation-based inference methods (e.g., BayesFlow) fitting separate single-subject models rather hierarchical approaches.

title: The Diffusion Decision Model (ddm)
text: simplest DDM drift, boundary, non-decision time: Interpreting fixed-zr model: drift: Higher values indicate faster evidence accumulation (easier trials) bound: Higher values indicate cautious responding ndt: Time spent non-decision processes
code: # Define the model model_fixed_zr <- ddm(rt = "rt",                        response = "response")  # Define the formula - let drift vary by strength formula_fixed_zr <- bmf(   drift ~ 0 + strength,   bound ~ 1,   ndt ~ 1 )  # Fit the model  fit_fixed_zr <- bmm(   formula = formula_fixed_zr,   data = demo_data,   model = model_fixed_zr,   backend = "cmdstanr",   cores = 4,   chains = 4,   iter = 2000,   warmup = 1000,   file = "assets/bmmfit_ddm_fixed_zr_vignette" )  # Examine convergence summary(fit_fixed_zr)  # Check diagnostics plot(fit_fixed_zr)

title: The Diffusion Decision Model (ddm)
text: Benefits hierarchical modeling: Partial pooling: Borrows strength across subjects better estimates Individual differences: Quantifies -subject variability Handles unbalanced data: Works even different trial counts per subject Shrinkage: Extreme individual estimates pulled toward group mean
code: # Use multiple subjects from rr98 multi_subject_data <- rr98 %>%   filter(instruction == "accuracy") %>%   mutate(response = ifelse(response_num == 1, 0, 1)) %>%   select(id, rt, response, strength)  # Hierarchical model model_hier <- ddm(rt = "rt",                    response = "response")  # Formula with random effects formula_hier <- bmf(   drift ~ 0 + strength + (0 + strength | id),   bound ~ 1 + (1 | id),   ndt ~ 1 + (1 | id) )  # Fit hierarchical model fit_hier <- bmm(   formula = formula_hier,   data = multi_subject_data,   model = model_hier,   backend = "cmdstanr",   cores = 4 )  # Extract individual-level parameters # This gives you person-specific drift, bound, and ndt estimates

   }   /* compute the tan_half link (vectorized)    * Args:    *   x: a vector in (-pi, pi)    * Returns:    *   a vector in (-Inf, Inf)    */    vector tan_half(vector x) {      return tan(x / 2);    }   /* compute the inverse of the tan_half link    * Args:    *   y: a scalar in (-Inf, Inf)    * Returns:    *   a scalar in (-pi, pi)    */    real inv_tan_half(real y) {      return 2 * atan(y);    }   /* compute the inverse of the tan_half link (vectorized)    * Args:    *   y: a vector in (-Inf, Inf)    * Returns:    *   a vector in (-pi, pi)    */    vector inv_tan_half(vector y) {      return 2 * atan(y);    }      // utility function trick for converting real to integer type   int bin_search(real x, int min_val, int max_val) {       int mid_p;       int L = min_val;       int R = max_val;       while(L < R) {         mid_p = (R-L) %/% 2;         if (L + mid_p < x) {           L += mid_p + 1;         } else if (L + mid_p > x) {           R = L + mid_p - 1;         } else {           return(L + mid_p);         }       }       return(L);     }    // utility function for determining optimal number of chebyshev points for the denominator approximation   int get_m(real c, real kappa) {     real m = floor(2 * exp(0.4*c) * kappa^(fma(c,0.0145,0.7)) + 0.5)+2;     int M = bin_search(m, 2, 200);     return(M);   }    // log of the numerator of the sdm likelihood   real sdm_simple_lpdf(vector y, vector mu, vector c, vector kappa) {     int N = size(y);     vector[N] num = exp(fma(kappa,cos(y-mu)-1,c)) ;     real out = dot_product(num, sqrt(kappa));     out *= inv(sqrt2()) * inv_sqrt(pi());     return(out);   }    // log of the normalization constant, approximated by chebyshev quadrature   real sdm_simple_ldenom_chquad_adaptive(real c, real kappa, matrix CN) {     int m = get_m(c,kappa);     vector[m] cosn = CN[1:m,m];     vector[m] fn = exp(fma(kappa,cosn,c)) * sqrt(kappa) * inv(sqrt2()) * inv_sqrt(pi());     real out = -log_sum_exp(fn)+log(m);     return(out);   } } data {   int<lower=1> N;  // total number of observations   vector[N] Y;  // response variable   int<lower=1> K_c;  // number of population-level effects   matrix[N, K_c] X_c;  // population-level design matrix   int<lower=1> K_kappa;  // number of population-level effects   matrix[N, K_kappa] X_kappa;  // population-level design matrix   int prior_only;  // should the likelihood be ignored? } transformed data {     // precompute chebyshev points   matrix[200,200] COSN;   for (m in 1:200) {     for (i in 1:m) {       COSN[i,m] = cos((2*i-1)*pi()/(2*m))-1;     }   } } parameters {   vector[K_c] b_c;  // regression coefficients   vector[K_kappa] b_kappa;  // regression coefficients } transformed parameters {   real Intercept;  // temporary intercept for centered predictors   // prior contributions to the log posterior   real lprior = 0;   Intercept = 0;   lprior += student_t_lpdf(b_c | 5, 2, 0.75);   lprior += student_t_lpdf(b_kappa | 5, 1.75, 0.75); } model {   // likelihood including constants   if (!prior_only) {     // initialize linear predictor term     vector[N] mu = rep_vector(0.0, N);     // initialize linear predictor term     vector[N] c = rep_vector(0.0, N);     // initialize linear predictor term     vector[N] kappa = rep_vector(0.0, N);     mu += Intercept;     c += X_c * b_c;     kappa += X_kappa * b_kappa;     mu = inv_tan_half(mu);     kappa = exp(kappa);     target += sdm_simple_lpdf(Y | mu, c, kappa);       // adaptive calculation of the normalization constant     real z;     for (n in 1:N) {         if (n == 1 || c[n] != c[n-1] || kappa[n] != kappa[n-1]) {             z = sdm_simple_ldenom_chquad_adaptive(c[n],kappa[n],COSN);         }         target += z;     }     target += -(log2()+log(pi()))*N;   }   // priors including constants   target += lprior; } generated quantities {   // actual population-level intercept   real b_Intercept = Intercept; } fit <- bmm(bmf(c ~ 0 + set_size, kappa ~ 0 + set_size),                data = oberauer_lin_2017,               model = sdm(resp_error = 'dev_rad')) stancode(fit)

title: The EZ-Diffusion Model (EZDM)
text: diffusion model (Ratcliff 1978) widely used model speeded decision-making. describes participants accumulate noisy evidence time reaching one two decision boundaries. Usually, diffusion model fit trial-level reaction time distributions, can computationally intensive, especially hierarchical Bayesian estimation. EZ-Diffusion Model (Wagenmakers et al. 2007) provides simplified alternative building closed-form equations relate parameters diffusion model easily computed summary statistics: mean reaction time (MRT), reaction time variance (VRT), accuracy (proportion correct, Pc). makes possible calculate diffusion model parameters aggregated data without fitting individual trials.

title: The EZ-Diffusion Model (EZDM)
text: standard diffusion model, evidence accumulates starting point toward one two boundaries. key parameters : Drift rate (\(v\)): average rate evidence accumulation, reflecting task difficulty ability Boundary separation (\(\)): distance two decision boundaries, reflecting speed-accuracy tradeoff Non-decision time (\(T_{er}\)): Time processes outside decision (encoding, motor response) Starting point (\(z\)): response bias indicating evidence accumulation begins relative boundaries Figure 1.1: Illustration diffusion model. Evidence accumulates starting point reaching upper (correct) lower (error) boundary.

title: The EZ-Diffusion Model (EZDM)
text: Wagenmakers et al. (2007) provided closed-form solutions relating diffusion model parameters observable summary statistics. 3-parameter version (assuming symmetric starting point, \(z = /2\)): Given proportion correct (\(P_c\)), mean RT correct responses (\(MRT\)), variance correct RTs (\(VRT\)), parameters can computed : \[ v = \text{sign}(P_c - 0.5) \cdot s \cdot \left[ L(P_c) \cdot \frac{P_c^2 L(P_c) - P_c \cdot L(P_c) + P_c - 0.5}{VRT} \right]^{1/4} \] \[ = s^2 \cdot \frac{L(P_c)}{v} \] \[ T_{er} = MRT - \frac{}{2v} \cdot \frac{1 - e^{-\frac{va}{s^2}}}{1 + e^{-\frac{va}{s^2}}} \] \(L(P_c) = \ln\left(\frac{P_c}{1 - P_c}\right)\) logit function \(s\) diffusion constant (typically fixed 1 identification).

title: The EZ-Diffusion Model (EZDM)
text: original EZ model assumes symmetric starting point. Srivastava et al. (2016) derived moments first-passage times Wiener diffusion process arbitrary starting points, enabling 4-parameter version can estimate starting point bias (\(z_r\), relative starting point). 4-parameter version, however, requires separate summary statistics responses boundary: Mean variance RTs upper boundary responses (typically correct) Mean variance RTs lower boundary responses (typically errors) sufficient responses upper lower bound, allows estimation response bias, important participants favor one response another.

Specifically, approach: Treats summary statistics observed data generated known sampling distribution Uses likelihood-based inference estimate parameters proper uncertainty quantification Enables hierarchical modeling random effects across participants Chávez De la Peña Vandekerckhove (2025) shared JAGS code alongside model. downside implementation model code adapted different experimental designs likely leads errors increases bar using implementation. bmm package implements Bayesian approach, allowing researchers : Estimate uncertainty parameter estimates Include random effects participants Compare conditions using Bayesian hypothesis testing Leverage full power brms modeling framework

title: Handling RT Contamination in Evidence Accumulation Models
text: Evidence accumulation models assume observed RTs arise single cognitive process. practice, trials reflect something else entirely: anticipatory responses, attention lapses, accidental button presses. Even contaminant trials can bias parameter estimates distort model fit (Ratcliff Tuerlinckx 2002). bmm package provides two functions dealing contamination, one type model supports: fit mixture model via EM algorithm, separating cognitive RTs uniform contaminant distribution (Ratcliff Tuerlinckx 2002): \[ f(RT) = (1 - \pi) \cdot f_{\text{cognitive}}(RT) + \pi \cdot f_{\text{uniform}}(RT) \] \(\pi\) contamination proportion. cognitive component \(f_{\text{cognitive}}\) can ex-Gaussian (default), log-normal, inverse Gaussian. background EZ diffusion model, see Wagenmakers et al. code: bmm <- function(formula, data, model,                 prior = NULL,                 sort_data = getOption('bmm.sort_data', "check"),                 silent = getOption('bmm.silent', 1),                 backend = getOption('brms.backend', NULL),                 file = NULL, file_compress = TRUE,                 file_refit = getOption('bmm.file_refit', FALSE), ...) {   deprecated_args(...)   dots <- list(...)    x <- read_bmmfit(file, file_refit)   if (!is.null(x)) return(x)    # set temporary global options and return modified arguments for brms   configure_opts <- nlist(sort_data, silent, backend, parallel = dots$parallel,                           cores = dots$cores)   opts <- configure_options(configure_opts)   dots$parallel <- NULL    # check model, formula and data, and transform data if necessary   user_formula <- formula   model <- check_model(model, data, formula)   data <- check_data(model, data, formula)   formula <- check_formula(model, data, formula)    # generate the model specification to pass to brms later   config_args <- configure_model(model, data, formula)    # configure the default prior and combine with user-specified prior   prior <- configure_prior(model, data, config_args$formula, prior)    # estimate the model   fit_args <- combine_args(nlist(config_args, opts, dots, prior))   fit <- call_brm(fit_args)    # model post-processing   fit <- postprocess_brm(model, fit, fit_args = fit_args, user_formula = user_formula,                          configure_opts = configure_opts)    # save the fitted model object if !is.null   save_bmmfit(fit, file, compress = file_compress) }

title: Test if fast contaminants show random guessing behavior — validate_fast_guesses
text: function performs Bayesian test using Beta-Binomial conjugate prior-posterior relationship. Beta(alpha, beta) prior observing n_upper "upper" responses n_tested trials, posterior : Beta(alpha + n_upper, beta + n_lower) Savage-Dickey Bayes Factor compares posterior prior densities null hypothesis value (default 0.5): BF_01 = posterior_density(guess_prob) / prior_density(guess_prob) Evidence categories follow Jeffreys (1961) scale: BF > 10: Strong evidence guessing BF > 3: Moderate evidence guessing BF > 1: Anecdotal evidence guessing BF < 1/3: Moderate evidence guessing BF < 1/10: Strong evidence guessing Note: function can used standalone validation step obtaining contamination probabilities flag_contaminant_rts().
